items.title: [Bug fix] moreh_clip_grad_norm: support norm_type inf, -inf and 0
items.body:
### PR Category
Bug fix

### Summary
Fixes #55587

`ttnn.operations.moreh.clip_grad_norm` accepted `norm_type = +inf`, `-inf` and `0` but fed them into the `Sum[|e|^p]^(1/p)` kernels, whose host-side decomposition (`floor`, `ord - floor(ord)`, `static_cast<uint32_t>`) is undefined for non-finite orders and whose step2 uses `1/norm_type`. The result was a total norm unrelated to the gradients (exactly `1.0`, or non-finite) and gradients silently rescaled by it.

This routes those three orders around step1/step2 and assembles the total norm from per-tensor `ttnn::moreh_norm` calls (which already implement them), combined with the same order the way `torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_` does (`torch.linalg.vector_norm(torch.stack(norms), norm_type)`):

- `+inf`: `ttnn::maximum` across tensors of `max|g|`
- `-inf`: `ttnn::minimum` across tensors of `min|g|`
- `0`: count of tensors with a nonzero per-tensor norm (`ttnn::nez` + `ttnn::add`)

The optional `total_norm` output tensor is honoured on that path via `ttnn::assign`; the existing `clip_coef` and step3 code is reused unchanged, and finite non-zero orders take exactly the same path as before.

Adds `test_moreh_clip_grad_norm_special_norm_type` (nightly) covering the three orders, both `max_norm` values, tile-aligned and padded shapes, with planted exact zeros so `-inf` and `0` exercise their edge values; gradients are round-tripped through bfloat16 so torch and ttnn see identical inputs (max/min are order statistics).

### Notes for reviewers
- Combining across tensors is a loop of tiny binary ops (one per input tensor) rather than a new multi-input kernel, mirroring the loops `moreh_norm` itself uses for multi-dim reductions. It is correct first; if the per-call cost matters for hundreds of parameters, a concat + single `moreh_norm` would be the follow-up.
- `ttnn::maximum` / `ttnn::minimum` drop NaN (#51470), so a NaN gradient under `norm_type=inf` may not propagate to `total_norm` the way torch's `max` does. Finite inputs are unaffected.
- I do not have device access; the host-side replay in #55587 is verified, the new test has not been run on silicon. Please let CI pick it up.

items.title: Support multi-batch prefill + decode on Blackhole devices

labels.name: feat
labels.description: New feature

items.body:
### Background
Relates to #55588.

A customer from Korea is asking for multi-batch support for GPT-OSS.

Current status of GPT-OSS is 

- batch=32 for WH Galaxy
- batch=1 for rest of the systems.

### Summary

This PR adds **multi-batch (any batch size ≤ 32) decode and much faster prefill** for GPT-OSS-20B and GPT-OSS-120B.

Implementation steps were:

1. Add multi-batch decode
2. Realize prefill is too slow for high number of batches
3. Optimize prefill kernels for high number of batches.

Tested on 8 * p150 system.

### Implementation details

- **Multi-user decode on single-row meshes**: all users are one 32-row tile run through the union of their active experts with `ttnn.sparse_matmul`; per-(user, expert) routing weights zero the rest. Fused `[gate | up]` weights, tuned Blackhole grids. → 120B 879 tok/s, 20B 1816 tok/s at batch 32; no cross-user leakage (PCC 1.000).
- **Any batch ≤ 32 on Blackhole**: per-user Q/K/V / KV-cache / SDPA core placement follows the RoPE placement and is checked at construction (the 13-wide grid otherwise mixes users).
- **Prefill MoE without `sparse_matmul` (EP=1)**: ≤ 256-token splits → one batched matmul per projection; longer splits → hot/cold expert-sorted MoE (hot experts dense, cold experts only over their `topk`-gathered rows, one-hot scatter back); fused single-op SwiGLU. Sparse path kept for EP > 1. → 120B TTFT 405 → 146 ms at ISL 128, 22.9 → 2.4 s at 8192; 20B 96 → 59 ms, 4.0 → 0.89 s.
- **Regression harness** `tests/test_multi_user_regression.py`: server benchmark pairs × batch {1..32} with quality gates and TTFT/decode metrics. → 105/105 cells pass, 0 hangs.

items.title: [ops]: ttnn.operations.moreh.clip_grad_norm silently mishandles norm_type = inf / -inf / 0: the p-decimal decomposition is undefined for them and step2 raises the sum to the power 0, while moreh_norm special-cases the same orders

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

items.body:
### Component / Area

ops (`ttnn.operations.moreh.clip_grad_norm`, `ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/moreh/moreh_clip_grad_norm`)

### Issue Type (optional)

Bad Outputs

### Observed

`ttnn.operations.moreh.clip_grad_norm(grads, max_norm, norm_type)` accepts any `norm_type` (the docstring only says "Type of the norm (e.g., 2.0 for L2 norm)"), but the three orders that are not a plain `Sum[|e|^p]^(1/p)` are silently mishandled: `float("inf")`, `float("-inf")` and `0.0`. `inf` is the second most common choice in practice (`torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(..., norm_type="inf")` / `max_grad_norm` with the infinity norm).

Both device steps decompose `norm_type` into an integer part, a fractional part and a sign:

```cpp
// moreh_clip_grad_norm_step1_program_factory.cpp L19-L25 (same helper duplicated in step2 L18-L24)
std::tuple<uint32_t, float, bool> get_p_decimal_p_is_negative(float ord) {
    auto p = std::floor(ord);
    auto fractional_part = ord - p;
    const bool p_is_negative = p < 0.0f;
    uint32_t integer_part = static_cast<uint32_t>(std::abs(p));
    return std::make_tuple(integer_part, fractional_part, p_is_negative);
}
```

and the kernels then compute `|x|^p * exp(log(|x|) * decimal)` per element (`moreh_common.hpp::power_tile_to_cb`, L887-L960, `power_iterative_tile(dst0, p)` at L908). That decomposition only makes sense for a finite non-zero order:

| `norm_type` | step1: `get_p_decimal_p_is_negative(norm_type)` | step2: `get_p_decimal_p_is_negative(1.0f / norm_type)` (L48) |
|---|---|---|
| `+inf` | `floor(inf) = inf`, `inf - inf = NaN`, `static_cast<uint32_t>(inf)` is undefined (`[conv.fpint]`) | `1/inf = 0` -> `p = 0`, `decimal = 0` -> `x^0 * exp(log(x) * 0) = 1` for every finite `x > 0` |
| `-inf` | same, plus `p_is_negative = true` | `1/-inf = -0.0` -> `p = 0`, `decimal = -0.0`, `p_is_negative = false` -> `1` |
| `0` | `p = 0`, `decimal = 0` -> every element (including the zeros the mask writes into tile padding) contributes `0^0 = 1`, so the per-tensor "sum" is the padded element count | `1/0 = inf` -> undefined integer part, `decimal = NaN` |

Consequences, following the code path element by element:

- `norm_type = inf` / `-inf`: step1 multiplies every element by `exp(log(|x|) * NaN)`, which is NaN by IEEE, and hands the kernel an undefined runtime `p` (the `power_iterative_tile` loop bound). Whatever the SFPU turns that into, step2 then raises it to the power `0`, so the reported `total_norm` is either exactly `1.0` (finite input to step2) or non-finite. It is never `max|g|` / `min|g|`. With `error_if_nonfinite=True` the op can raise the misleading "The total norm of order inf for gradients from `parameters` is non-finite" error for perfectly finite gradients; with the default `False` it silently rescales every gradient by `max_norm / (1.0 + 1e-6)` (L128-L129), i.e. it multiplies all gradients by `max_norm` regardless of their size, or by NaN.
- `norm_type = 0`: the per-tensor count is the padded element count instead of the nonzero count, and step2 gets an undefined integer part and a NaN decimal.

The only guard in the host op is `error_if_nonfinite && std::isnan(norm_type)` (`moreh_clip_grad_norm.cpp` L59); `inf` and `0` pass straight through. The sibling op `ttnn::moreh_norm` special-cases exactly these three orders on the host (`moreh_norm.cpp` L30 and L45, dispatching to the `MINUS_INF` / max / nonzero-count kernels), so the building blocks exist; `clip_grad_norm` just never routes to them. The nightly test only covers `norm_type in [2.0, -0.8, 2.2]` (`test_moreh_clip_grad_norm.py` L28), which is why this went unnoticed.

Concrete example (bfloat16, two gradients, `max_norm = 1.0`, `norm_type = inf`):

```text
g1 = [[ 3.0, -1.0, 0.5, 0.25]]     max|g1| = 3.0
g2 = [[-0.25, 0.125, 0.0, 0.0]]    max|g2| = 0.25

torch  total_norm = 3.0        clip_coef = 1/(3+1e-6)     g1 -> [ 1.0, -0.333, 0.167, 0.083]
ttnn   total_norm = 1.0 (*)    clip_coef = 1/(1+1e-6)     g1 -> [ 3.0, -1.0,   0.5,   0.25 ]  (unclipped)
(*) or NaN / an SFPU-dependent value, see above; in no branch of the code is it 3.0
```

### Expected

`torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_` semantics (`torch.linalg.vector_norm(torch.stack([vector_norm(g, norm_type) for g in grads]), norm_type)`):

- `+inf`: `total_norm = max over tensors of max|g|`
- `-inf`: `total_norm = min over tensors of min|g|`
- `0`: `total_norm = number of tensors whose count of nonzero elements is nonzero`

and the gradients scaled in place by `min(1, max_norm / (total_norm + 1e-6))`, exactly as for `norm_type = 2.0`.

### 1. Steps (exact commands)

Host-only replay of the host-side decomposition and of what the kernels are then asked to compute (no device needed, `pip install torch`):

```python
import math
import torch

def get_p_decimal_p_is_negative(ord):
    # moreh_clip_grad_norm_step1_program_factory.cpp L19-L25 / step2 L18-L24
    p = math.floor(ord) if math.isfinite(ord) else ord
    fractional_part = ord - p
    p_is_negative = p < 0.0
    integer_part = "UB (static_cast<uint32_t> of a non-representable value)" if not math.isfinite(p) else int(abs(p))
    return integer_part, fractional_part, p_is_negative

def step2_scalar(x, p, decimal, p_is_negative):
    # power_tile_to_cb: x^p * exp(log(x) * decimal), IEEE semantics for the transcendental steps
    xpow = x ** p if isinstance(p, int) else float("nan")
    if p_is_negative:
        xpow = 1.0 / xpow
    return xpow * math.exp(math.log(x) * decimal)

for norm_type in (float("inf"), float("-inf"), 0.0):
    print(f"norm_type = {norm_type}")
    print("  step1 (p, decimal, p_is_negative):", get_p_decimal_p_is_negative(norm_type))
    inv = 1.0 / norm_type if norm_type != 0.0 else float("inf")
    p, decimal, neg = get_p_decimal_p_is_negative(inv)
    print("  step2 (p, decimal, p_is_negative):", (p, decimal, neg))
    if isinstance(p, int):
        print("  step2 total_norm for a finite positive Sum[...] of 9.0:", step2_scalar(9.0, p, decimal, neg))

g1 = torch.tensor([[3.0, -1.0, 0.5, 0.25]], dtype=torch.bfloat16)
g2 = torch.tensor([[-0.25, 0.125, 0.0, 0.0]], dtype=torch.bfloat16)
for norm_type in (float("inf"), float("-inf"), 0.0):
    params = []
    for g in (g1, g2):

        p.grad = g.clone()
        params.append(p)
    total = torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, 1.0, norm_type)
    print(f"torch norm_type={norm_type}: total_norm={total.item()}  g1 after clip={params[0].grad.tolist()}")
```

Output of the replay:

```text
norm_type = inf
  step1 (p, decimal, p_is_negative): ('UB (static_cast<uint32_t> of a non-representable value)', nan, False)
  step2 (p, decimal, p_is_negative): (0, 0.0, False)
  step2 total_norm for a finite positive Sum[...] of 9.0: 1.0
norm_type = -inf
  step1 (p, decimal, p_is_negative): ('UB (static_cast<uint32_t> of a non-representable value)', nan, True)
  step2 (p, decimal, p_is_negative): (0, -0.0, False)
  step2 total_norm for a finite positive Sum[...] of 9.0: 1.0
norm_type = 0.0
  step1 (p, decimal, p_is_negative): (0, 0.0, False)
  step2 (p, decimal, p_is_negative): ('UB (static_cast<uint32_t> of a non-representable value)', nan, False)
torch norm_type=inf: total_norm=3.0  g1 after clip=[[1.0, -0.333984375, 0.1669921875, 0.08349609375]]

torch norm_type=0.0: total_norm=2.0  g1 after clip=[[1.5, -0.5, 0.25, 0.125]]
```

On a card, the same thing as a test:

```bash
pytest tests/ttnn/nightly/unit_tests/operations/moreh/test_moreh_clip_grad_norm.py -k special_norm_type
```

(that test is on the branch linked below; on `main` the equivalent is to call `ttnn.operations.moreh.clip_grad_norm([ttnn.from_torch(g1, layout=ttnn.TILE_LAYOUT, device=device), ttnn.from_torch(g2, ...)], 1.0, float("inf"))` and compare against the torch values above).

### 2. Input data / link or description

Inline in the snippet above. Source references are against `main` @ 28238f903b3c35d2f6c91c99d3d249b3db843076:

- `ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/moreh/moreh_clip_grad_norm/moreh_clip_grad_norm.cpp` L59 (only NaN is rejected), L92 / L108 (step1 / step2 dispatch), L128-L129 (`clip_coef`)
- `.../moreh_clip_grad_norm_step1/device/moreh_clip_grad_norm_step1_program_factory.cpp` L19-L25, L63
- `.../moreh_clip_grad_norm_step2/device/moreh_clip_grad_norm_step2_program_factory.cpp` L18-L24, L48 (`1.0f / norm_type`)
- `.../moreh_clip_grad_norm_step1/device/kernels/moreh_clip_grad_norm_step1_kernel.cpp` L14-L15, L106; `.../step2/.../moreh_clip_grad_norm_step2_kernel.cpp` L11-L12, L81
- `ttnn/cpp/ttnn/kernel/compute/moreh_common.hpp` L887-L960 (`power_tile_to_cb`)
- `ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/moreh/moreh_norm/moreh_norm.cpp` L30, L45 (the sibling op's handling of the same orders)
- `tests/ttnn/nightly/unit_tests/operations/moreh/test_moreh_clip_grad_norm.py` L28

### 3. Frequency

Always (deterministic; it is the host-side argument decomposition, independent of the data).

### 1. Software Versions

Source-level analysis of `main` @ 28238f903b3c35d2f6c91c99d3d249b3db843076 (2026-09-06). The host-side replay above needs only Python 3 + torch (verified with torch 2.11).

### 2. Hardware Details

Not run on silicon: I do not have a card, so I have not asserted which of the two failure modes (`total_norm == 1.0` vs. a non-finite / SFPU-flushed value) appears on Wormhole or Blackhole. The defect is in the host decomposition and is architecture independent.

### Is this a regression?

Unknown

### Regression Details

The helper and the `1.0f / norm_type` call date back to the original `moreh_clip_grad_norm` implementation; there was never an `inf` / `0` path.

### Logs & Diagnostics

n/a (see replay output above)

### Priority

P2

### Impact

Any training loop using the infinity norm for gradient clipping (`norm_type="inf"`) gets its gradients scaled by `max_norm` (or NaN) instead of being clipped, with no warning. `error_if_nonfinite=True` can turn finite gradients into a hard error.

### Proposed fix

Route `norm_type in {+inf, -inf, 0}` around the step1/step2 kernels and build the total norm from per-tensor `ttnn::moreh_norm` calls (which already implement these orders), combined with the same order the way torch does: `ttnn::maximum` across tensors for `+inf`, `ttnn::minimum` for `-inf`, and the count of tensors with a nonzero per-tensor norm (`ttnn::nez` + `ttnn::add`) for `0`. The optional `total_norm` output tensor is honoured on that path with `ttnn::assign`, and the existing `clip_coef` / step3 code is reused unchanged.

Implemented, with a nightly test for the three orders (`test_moreh_clip_grad_norm_special_norm_type`), on https://github.com/raunitgrey7/tt-metal/tree/fix/moreh-clip-grad-norm-inf-zero-order (diff: https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/compare/main...raunitgrey7:tt-metal:fix/moreh-clip-grad-norm-inf-zero-order). I would like to be assigned to this issue and will open the PR from that branch.

items.title: [Bug] moreh_norm_backward returns NaN for all-zero reduced slices, where the gradient is finite

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

items.body:
## Summary

`ttnn.operations.moreh.norm_backward` computes the gradient of `norm(x, p, dim)` as

```
dx = sign(x) * |x|^(p-1) * y * dy * (1 / y^p)        where y = norm(x, p, dim)
```

with no guard for `y == 0`. When a reduced slice is entirely zero its norm is
zero, `1 / y^p` is non-finite, and it multiplies a zero factor, so every element
of that slice comes back non-finite. PyTorch returns a finite `0`.

```
input:    [[0, 0, 0],
           [1, 2, 2]]
p:        2.0
dim:      1
grad:     [1, 1]

norm:     [0, 3]
expected: [[0,      0,      0     ],   <- PyTorch
           [0.3333, 0.6667, 0.6667]]
current:  [[non-finite, non-finite, non-finite],
           [0.3333,     0.6667,     0.6667    ]]
```

An all-zero reduced slice is not exotic: zero-initialised embedding rows, padded
or fully-masked sequence positions, and dead channels all produce one. A single
non-finite gradient propagates through the optimiser and destroys the whole
parameter tensor on the next step.

The same missing guard also affects `p < 1` with an exactly-zero *element*, even
when the slice's norm is non-zero: `|0|^(p-1)` is non-finite there, and PyTorch
masks that case too (see below).

## Root cause

`ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/moreh/moreh_norm_backward/device/kernels/moreh_norm_backward_kernel.cpp`

```
L50   sign  = sign_tile(x)
L53   xpow  = |x|^(p-1)          power_tile_with_abs_x_to_cb
L63   tmp4  = xpow * y
L90   tmp5  = tmp4 * dy
L118  recip = 1 / y^p            power_and_recip_tile_to_cb
L128  tmp4  = tmp5 * recip
L160  dx    = sign * tmp4        mul_tiles_to_cb
```

`power_and_recip_tile_to_cb`
(`ttnn/cpp/ttnn/kernel/compute/moreh_common.hpp`) ends in a `recip_tile` on
`y^p`. For `y == 0` that reciprocal is non-finite, and the surrounding factors
(`xpow`, `y`, and `sign` — all zero when the slice is all zeros) are exactly the
zeros that turn it into a NaN rather than cancelling it.

There is no `y == 0` guard anywhere on the path:

- the compute kernel above,
- `.../device/moreh_norm_backward_program_factory.cpp`,
- `.../device/moreh_norm_backward_device_operation.cpp`,
- `.../moreh_norm_backward.cpp` (host entry, forwards straight to `ttnn::prim`).

PyTorch derives the same formula but zeroes the singular cases explicitly.
`torch/csrc/autograd/FunctionsManual.cpp`, `norm_backward` (quoting v2.11.0,
the version pinned in `tt_metal/python_env/requirements-dev.txt`):

```cpp
} else if (p == 2.0) {
    return grad * (self / norm).masked_fill_(norm == 0, 0);
} else if (p < 1.0) {
    self_scaled = self.sgn() * self.abs().pow_(p - 1).masked_fill_(self == 0, 0);
    return self_scaled * grad * norm.pow(1 - p);
} else if (p < 2.0) {
    self_scaled = self.sgn() * self.abs().pow_(p - 1);
    scale_v = grad / norm.pow(p - 1);
    scale_v.masked_fill_(norm == 0, 0);
    return self_scaled * scale_v;
} else {
    self_scaled = self * self.abs().pow_(p - 2);
    scale_v = grad / norm.pow(p - 1);
    scale_v.masked_fill_(norm == 0, 0);
    ...
```

Every branch carries a `masked_fill_`. That is the piece tt-metal inlined away.

Unlike a reduction that loses information (the `prod_bw` zero case, for
instance), nothing here is unrecoverable — the correct answer is simply `0`, and
the formula fails only because `0 * inf` is NaN. So the fix is cheap. Two
caveats on how to apply it:

- Clamping `y` to some `eps` before the reciprocal is enough for `p >= 1`, since
  the `|x|^(p-1)` factor is itself `0` there and kills the large reciprocal.
- It is *not* enough for `p < 1`, where `|0|^(p-1)` is itself non-finite and no
  clamp on `y` can rescue it. That branch needs the element-wise
  `where(x == 0, 0, ...)` that PyTorch applies.

An explicit `where(norm == 0, 0, dx)` covers both and mirrors PyTorch directly,
which also keeps the intent legible: `0` here is the sub-gradient chosen by
convention at a point where the norm is not differentiable, not a limit of the
formula.

For contrast, `moreh_clip_grad_norm` in this same family *does* carry the
corresponding guard (`moreh_clip_grad_norm.cpp:126-129`, `max_norm / (total_norm
+ 1e-6)`), which suggests the omission in `norm_backward` is an oversight rather
than a deliberate contract.

## Reproducer

I do not have a card. This is a source-level analysis: the script below replays
the kernel's arithmetic on the host in fp32 and compares it against PyTorch
autograd. It does not exercise the device.

```
pip install "torch==2.11.0"
python repro_moreh_norm_backward.py
```

```python
import numpy as np, torch
f32 = np.float32

def ttnn_moreh_norm_backward(x, y, dy, p):
    """Replay of moreh_norm_backward_kernel.cpp in fp32.
    x: input (..., N)   y: forward norm, keepdim (..., 1)   dy: grad (..., 1)"""
    x, y, dy = x.astype(f32), y.astype(f32), dy.astype(f32)
    with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore", over="ignore"):
        sign = np.sign(x).astype(f32)
        xpow = np.power(np.abs(x), f32(p - 1.0)).astype(f32)   # |x|^(p-1)
        tmp4 = (xpow * y).astype(f32)
        tmp5 = (tmp4 * dy).astype(f32)
        recip = (f32(1.0) / np.power(y, f32(p))).astype(f32)   # 1 / y^p
        return (sign * (tmp5 * recip)).astype(f32)

x  = np.array([[0., 0., 0.], [1., 2., 2.], [0., 3., 4.]], dtype=f32)
for p in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0):
    y  = np.linalg.norm(x.astype(np.float64), ord=p, axis=1, keepdims=True).astype(f32)
    dy = np.ones_like(y)
    tt = ttnn_moreh_norm_backward(x, y, dy, p)

    t = torch.tensor(x, requires_grad=True)
    torch.linalg.vector_norm(t, ord=p, dim=1, keepdim=True).backward(torch.tensor(dy))
    ref = t.grad.numpy()

    print(f"p={p:<5} ttnn non-finite: {int((~np.isfinite(tt)).sum())}  "
          f"torch non-finite: {int((~np.isfinite(ref)).sum())}")
```

Output (torch 2.11.0+cpu):

```
p=0.5   ttnn non-finite: 4  torch non-finite: 0
p=1.0   ttnn non-finite: 3  torch non-finite: 0
p=2.0   ttnn non-finite: 3  torch non-finite: 0
p=2.5   ttnn non-finite: 3  torch non-finite: 0
p=3.0   ttnn non-finite: 3  torch non-finite: 0
```

The three are the all-zero row. The fourth at `p = 0.5` is the exact zero in row
`[0, 3, 4]`, which is the `masked_fill_(self == 0, 0)` branch PyTorch takes for
`p < 1`.

Per-element table for `p = 2.0`:

```
input row    norm    ttnn dx                    torch dx
[0, 0, 0]    0       [nan, nan, nan]            [0, 0, 0]          <- diverges
[1, 2, 2]    3       [0.3333, 0.6667, 0.6667]   [same]             ok
[0, 3, 4]    5       [0, 0.6, 0.8]              [same]             ok
```

Two things I could **not** verify without hardware, stated as open questions
rather than claims:

1. Whether the SFPU yields NaN or ±inf here. The host replay gives NaN. Either
   way the result is non-finite where PyTorch is finite, since nothing on the
   path can produce `0`; but I cannot confirm which.
2. `power_tile_with_abs_x_to_cb` evaluates `exp(log|x| * decimal)` unconditionally,
   and `decimal` is `0` for integer `p`. If the SFPU's `log(0)` returns `-inf`,
   then `-inf * 0` is NaN and `|x|^(p-1)` would be NaN at *every* exactly-zero
   element, not only in all-zero slices — widening the blast radius considerably.
   If `log_tile` instead saturates to a finite negative value, this second effect
   does not occur and only the all-zero-slice case above applies. I have no way
   to tell which from the source alone.

## Additional observation: `p = ±inf` on the backward path

Not the subject of this report, but it surfaced while reading the same code and
seems worth recording here rather than in a separate issue.

`moreh_norm_backward_program_factory.cpp:37-45` decomposes `p` with

```cpp
std::tuple<uint32_t, float, bool> get_floored_p_and_decimal_and_p_is_negative(float p) {
    auto floored_p = std::floor(p);
    auto decimal = p - floored_p;
    ...
    return std::make_tuple(static_cast<uint32_t>(floored_p), decimal, p_is_negative);
}
```

For `p = ±inf` this evaluates `static_cast<uint32_t>(std::floor(inf))`, which is
undefined behaviour for an out-of-range floating-to-integer conversion, and
`decimal = inf - inf = NaN`. There is also no `isinf(p)` branch in the compute
kernel, whereas PyTorch's `norm_backward` has a dedicated one (the `argmax` mask
over `self.abs() == norm`).

The forward test parametrises `p` over `[2.0, 2.5, -2.5, 0.0, inf, -inf]`, but
the backward test
(`test_moreh_norm.py`, `test_moreh_norm_backward`) only covers
`[2.0, 2.5, -2.5]`, so neither `±inf` nor `0.0` is exercised on this path. For
reference, torch 2.11.0 returns finite gradients for `p = ±inf` and no gradient
at all for `p = 0` (`norm_backward` returns `{}`). I have not tried to
characterise what the current kernel does for these values — I only want to flag
that they appear to be unhandled and untested.

## Expected behavior

Match `norm_backward`: where the norm of a slice is zero, the gradient for every
element of that slice is `0`.

- **no zeros in the slice** — current behaviour is already correct.
- **some zeros, norm > 0** — the host replay comes out correct for `p >= 1`
  (`sign(0) = 0` absorbs the result), though see open question 2 above: on device
  this depends on what `log_tile(0)` returns. For `p < 1`, elements that are
  exactly zero should be forced to `0` (PyTorch's
  `.masked_fill_(self == 0, 0)`), not `|0|^(p-1)`.
- **whole slice zero, norm == 0** — every element of the slice should be `0`.
  Currently non-finite.

Concretely, the kernel needs the equivalent of `where(y == 0, 0, dx)` applied
after the reciprocal-multiply, broadcast over the reduced dimension, plus a
`where(x == 0, 0, xpow)` on the `p < 1` path.

## Suggested tests

`tests/ttnn/nightly/unit_tests/operations/moreh/test_moreh_norm.py` builds its
inputs with `make_torch_tensors`:

```python
torch_input = torch.empty(input_shape, dtype=dtype).uniform_(-1, 1).requires_grad_()
```

A continuous uniform draw makes an all-zero reduced slice a probability-zero
event, so `norm == 0` is never exercised — which is why this has stayed hidden.
Worth adding to `run_moreh_norm_backward`:

1. An input with at least one all-zero slice along the reduced dim, asserting the
   gradient is finite and exactly zero there, for `p` in
   `{0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, inf}`.
2. An all-zero input tensor (every slice degenerate).
3. For `p < 1`, a slice mixing exact zeros with non-zeros, asserting the zero
   positions get `0` rather than a non-finite value.
4. A `torch.isfinite(...).all()` assertion in `run_moreh_norm_backward`
   generally — `comp_allclose` currently compares values but the existing
   generator never produces the degenerate inputs that would trip it.

## One question before I go further

I would like to pick this up and submit a fix, and I understand I need to be
assigned first.

I noticed #46147 proposes documenting moreh ops as deprecated. Before I invest
in a fix, could you confirm whether `moreh_norm_backward` is still in scope for
the bounty program?

Happy to write the patch and the tests above as soon as I hear back.

items.title: [ttnn/data_movement] transpose/permute WH on RM + HEIGHT-sharded in → WIDTH-sharded out: silent all-zero output (num_hw_blocks_per_core=0)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

items.body:
## Summary

`ttnn.transpose(x, -2, -1)` (and `ttnn.permute(x, (0,1,3,2))` which routes through it) silently returns wrong data when the input is **ROW_MAJOR + HEIGHT_SHARDED** and the output is (either inherited or explicitly requested) **WIDTH_SHARDED**. No error, no fatal — just an output tensor with PCC ≈ 0 against torch.

Discovered via the TM Layout/Sharding audit under #25529 (§4.1). Not covered by #51214 (static-audit list).

## Repro (wormhole_b0, `main @ 6503ed3d720`)

```python
import torch, ttnn
def hs(cores, sh, sw):
    grid = ttnn.CoreRangeSet({ttnn.CoreRange(ttnn.CoreCoord(0,0), ttnn.CoreCoord(cores-1,0))})
    return ttnn.MemoryConfig(
        ttnn.TensorMemoryLayout.HEIGHT_SHARDED, ttnn.BufferType.L1,
        ttnn.ShardSpec(grid, (sh, sw), ttnn.ShardOrientation.ROW_MAJOR),
    )
d = ttnn.open_device(device_id=0)
torch.manual_seed(0)
t = torch.randn(1, 1, 64, 128, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
for cores in (2, 4, 8):
    x = ttnn.from_torch(t, layout=ttnn.ROW_MAJOR_LAYOUT, device=d,
                        memory_config=hs(cores, 64 // cores, 128))
    o_bad = ttnn.transpose(x, -2, -1)                                # inherits WIDTH_SHARDED
    o_ok  = ttnn.transpose(x, -2, -1, memory_config=ttnn.DRAM_MEMORY_CONFIG)
    print(cores, "bad", torch.corrcoef(torch.stack([
        ttnn.to_torch(o_bad).float().flatten(),
        t.transpose(-2,-1).contiguous().float().flatten()]))[0,1].item())
```

Result:

| cores | inherited-out PCC | DRAM_IL PCC |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | **0.0118** 🐞 | 1.0000 ✅ |
| 4 | **0.0097** 🐞 | 1.0000 ✅ |
| 8 | **-0.0003** 🐞 | 1.0000 ✅ |

`ttnn.permute(x, (0,1,3,2))` reproduces (PCC 0.0037 / 0.0017 / nan) since `permute.cpp:99-101` delegates to `ttnn::transpose(-2, -1)`.

## Root cause

Routing in `transpose_device_operation.cpp:130-131`:

```
bool use_sharded_wh =
    native && ((input_width_and_height_fully_in_shard && output_width_and_height_fully_in_shard) ||
               (N == 1 && C == 1 && input_height_sharded && output_width_sharded));
```

The second disjunct admits cases where `shard_shape[0] < H` (i.e. the H dim is split across cores) and, on RM, forwards to `TransposeWHShardedRMProgramFactory`. That factory computes:

```
transpose_wh_sharded_rm_program_factory.cpp:76
uint32_t num_hw_blocks_per_core = shard_height / H;   // truncates to 0 when shard_height < H
```

`num_hw_blocks_per_core = 0` is passed as compile-time arg 0 to reader / writer / compute kernels (lines 170, 191, 213); every per-core outer loop is `for (n = 0; n < num_hw_blocks_per_core; …)` and never executes, leaving the output CB unpopulated. Matches the sibling `transpose_hc_sharded_program_factory.cpp:124` which already clamps: `shard_height / H > 0 ? shard_height / H : 1`.

## Suggested fix

Either

1. Tighten routing — gate the RM branch of `use_sharded_wh` on `input_width_and_height_fully_in_shard && output_width_and_height_fully_in_shard`, so the H-split case falls through to `TransposeWHProgramFactory` (verified correct at PCC 1.0 for the same input in this repro).
2. Fix the factory to handle `shard_height < H` (bigger surgery; unnecessary if #1 lands since `TransposeWHProgramFactory` already covers this shape).

Preferred: #1.

## Test gap

`tests/ttnn/nightly/unit_tests/operations/data_movement/test_universal_input_tm_tranpose.py`'s RM matrix (lines 423-500) has entries for `block→interleaved`, `width→interleaved`, `interleaved→block`, `interleaved→width`, `block→block`, `height→interleaved` — no `height→width` RM cell. That is the exact cell that returns garbage.

## Related

- Parent tracker: #25529 (audit), #31716 (universal-input TMs)
- Not in #51214 defect list
- Same audit calls out three sibling silent-corruption bugs: clone DRAM_H-sharded (§4.2), move sharded-out (§4.3), untilize_with_unpadding BLOCK/ND-sharded-out (§4.4) — separate issues.

items.title: Bug fix: remainder returns the divisor for a negative zero dividend

labels.name: pr-priority:p2
labels.description: P2: Important but contained; workaround-supported, exploratory, or not actively blocking.

labels.name: pr-risk:medium
labels.description: Risk Medium: Meaningful but contained impact in a subsystem, workflow, model, or team.

labels.name: pr-complexity:low
labels.description: Complexity Low: Focused, established pattern with simple validation.

items.body:
### PR Category

Bug fix

### Summary

`ttnn.remainder` returns the divisor instead of zero when the dividend is negative zero. On Blackhole, float32 and bfloat16:

| call | before | torch |
|---|---|---|
| `remainder(-0.0, 2.0)` | `2.0` | `-0.0` |
| `remainder(-0.0, 3.0)` | `3.0` | `-0.0` |
| `remainder(-0.0, 0.5)` | `0.5` | `-0.0` |
| `remainder(-0.0, 7.25)` | `7.25` | `-0.0` |

The result is the whole divisor, so the error is full magnitude rather than a sign nit, and it grows with `b`.

The cause is the zero guard on the sign correction in `_sfpu_binary_remainder_`:

```cpp
v_if(result != 0.0f) {
    sfpi::vInt signs = sfpi::as<sfpi::vInt>(result) ^ sfpi::as<sfpi::vInt>(b);
    v_and(signs < 0);
    result += b;
}
```

`SFPSETCC` is unspecified for negative zero, since `VectorUnit.md` specifies the compare only for inputs that are neither negative zero nor NaN. `fmod` correctly leaves `-0.0` in `result`, the guard then admits it, `0x80000000 ^ as_int(b)` is negative for `b > 0`, and the correction adds `b` to an answer that was already right. Only positive divisors trip it, because the correction is gated on `result` and `b` disagreeing in the sign bit.

`sfpi::abs` clears the sign bit before the compare, so both zeros skip the correction and the comparison is back inside the specified contract. This is the same mechanism and the same remedy as #55306.

### Notes for reviewers

Wormhole did not show the defect before this change, but not because its guard was correct. The two architectures carry the same logic here, differing only in how the zero literal is spelled (`0.0f` on Blackhole, `sfpi::vFloat(0.0f)` on Wormhole), so each file keeps its own spelling in this change. Wormhole's `fmod` flushes every negative zero result to `+0.0`, so the guard receives `+0.0`, where the compare is well defined, and correctly skips. The hazard is present in the Wormhole source as well, masked by a separate deviation, so the guard is fixed on both architectures to keep them from diverging if that ever changes.

Verified on Blackhole p150b and Wormhole n150. After the fix Blackhole returns `0x80000000`, bit-exact with torch. `tests/ttnn/unit_tests/operations/eltwise/test_div_ops.py` passes at 118 passed, 8 skipped, 2 xfailed on both cards, and a 90 pair sweep of ordinary dividends and divisors is unchanged either side of the change.

The new test fails on both dtypes without the kernel change and passes with it.

Only the float32 and bfloat16 path is touched. Integer remainder dispatches to `remainder_int32_tile` and `remainder_uint32_tile` and is not affected.

items.body:
### PR Category
Bug fix

### Summary
Closes #55129.

On the fp32 path `ttnn.pow` returned `+inf` for every base once `|exponent| > FLT_MAX/4097`, including cases IEEE fixes exactly: `pow(1.0, 1e35)` gave `inf` instead of `1.0`, and `pow(0.5, 1e35)` gave `inf` instead of `0.0`.

The Veltkamp split multiplies the exponent by 4097 before decomposing it, so `pc` overflows to `inf`, `pc - (pc - pow)` becomes `inf - inf = NaN`, and the NaN reaches the final overflow guard as a biased exponent of 255, which turns every lane into `+inf`. This skips the decomposition where it cannot be represented: such an exponent drives `pow*log2(base)` far outside the `2**z` range for every base except 1, where `exp_f32` and `ln_m` are both zero, so the split has nothing to preserve. The threshold is exponent 115 rather than 116 because `FLT_MAX/4097 = 8.305647e34` falls inside `[2**115, 2**116)`, so a 116 guard would leave `[8.305647e34, 8.307675e34)` still overflowing. Applied to the binary and unary kernels on both architectures, which carry the same three lines.

Verified on ttsim (Blackhole, `v0.79.0-dev20260903`): of 17 cases spanning the band, 10 were wrong before and 1 after. On 1024 random ordinary inputs the results are bit-identical before and after, `max_rel 2.643e-07` on the tensor-tensor path and `2.220e-07` on `x**2.5`, so nothing outside the band moves.

### Notes for reviewers
The one case still wrong is `pow(-1.0, 1e35)`, which returns NaN where IEEE gives 1.0. That is a different mechanism: the negative-base path decides integer parity with `convert<vSMag16>`, and a 16-bit conversion cannot represent an exponent that large. It returned `inf` before this change and NaN after, both wrong, and I have left it alone rather than widen the scope.

items.body:
### PR Category

Bug fix

### Summary

`ttnn.is_real` and `ttnn.is_imag` have never been validated. Their golden functions raise,
and their sweeps compare all-false against all-false.

**1. Both goldens call torch functions that do not exist.**

`ttnn/ttnn/operations/unary_complex.py` had:

```python
return torch.is_imag(input_tensor_a)   # AttributeError
return torch.is_real(input_tensor_a)   # AttributeError
```

There is no `torch.is_imag` or `torch.is_real`. The real spelling is `torch.isreal`, and
there is no elementwise `isimag`. Any call through `ttnn.get_golden_function(...)` for
either op fails before a comparison happens, so neither has ever been checked against a
reference.

The device semantics come from `complex_unary_op.cpp`:

```cpp
Tensor _is_imag(...) { return ttnn::eqz(input[0]); }   // real part zero
Tensor _is_real(...) { return ttnn::eqz(input[1]); }   // imag part zero
```

so the goldens become `torch.real(x) == 0` and `torch.isreal(x)` respectively.

**2. The `is_imag` sweep used the wrong predicate.**

`tests/sweep_framework/sweeps/eltwise/unary_complex/is_imag.py` computed its reference with
`torch.isreal(...)`, which tests the imaginary part. `ttnn.is_imag` tests the real part.
Those are different predicates: on a mixed input they disagree on half the elements.

**3. Neither sweep could ever fail.**

`is_imag` drew both the real and imaginary parts from `torch_random(low=0.01, high=100)`,
so the real part was never zero and the op could never return true. `is_real` drew its
imaginary part from `torch_random(low=100, high=100)`, a constant 100, so the imaginary
part was never zero either. Both sweeps compared an all-false reference against an
all-false result and passed without exercising anything.

This PR fixes the two goldens, corrects the `is_imag` reference, and zeroes every other
column of the relevant part in both sweeps so the predicate is actually true for half the
elements.

### Testing

Both ops are correct; only the validation around them was broken. On Blackhole p150b, with
a mixed input where the predicate holds for half the elements:

```
is_imag  golden vs device: wrong 0/1024  true_count=512  MATCH
is_real  golden vs device: wrong 0/1024  true_count=512  MATCH
old is_imag reference (torch.isreal) vs correct predicate: differs on 512/1024 elements
```

So the fixed goldens agree with the device exactly on inputs that exercise them, and the
previous reference is measurably the wrong function.

Ran the repo pre-commit hooks over all three files; black, trailing whitespace, end of
files and the rest pass.

### PR Category
Bug fix

### Summary
Fixes #55576.

`ttnn.repeat_interleave` crashed for a **ROW_MAJOR, rank-4, DRAM-sharded** input. The native fast-path expresses ROW_MAJOR 4D `repeat_interleave` via `ttnn::upsample(..., "nearest")`, and it routed *any* sharded ROW_MAJOR-4D input into `upsample`. But `upsample`'s sharded kernel borrows its input directly as an L1 circular buffer and hard-requires an **L1-resident** input, so a DRAM-sharded input hit:

```
TT_FATAL: DFB 'upsample_shard_in' ... its TensorSpec is not L1-resident (L1 is required).
```

The fix adds an `is_l1()` guard to the fast-path condition so a **DRAM-sharded** input falls through to the existing interleaved round-trip fallback (unshard to interleaved DRAM -> run -> restore requested config) - the same path TILE DRAM-sharded inputs already use successfully:

```cpp
if (input_a.layout() == Layout::ROW_MAJOR && rank == 4 && input_a.memory_config().is_l1()) {
```

Scope of impact: only ROW_MAJOR 4D DRAM-sharded inputs were affected. L1-sharded (HEIGHT/WIDTH/BLOCK) and TILE DRAM-sharded inputs were already correct.


### Notes for reviewers
The one-line behavioral change is the `&& input_a.memory_config().is_l1()` guard in `repeat_interleave_native` ([repeat_interleave.cpp](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/abdulla/repeate_interleaved_DRAM_shard_fix/ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/data_movement/repeat_interleave/repeat_interleave.cpp)). items.body:
### PR Category

Bug fix

### Summary

`torch_random_with_zeros()` in `models/common/utility_functions.py` takes a `dtype`
argument and then discards the conversion:

```python
result_tensor = shuffled.view(shape)
result_tensor.to(dtype)      # return value dropped; Tensor.to is not in-place
return result_tensor
```

`shuffled` comes from `torch.empty(...).uniform_()` and `torch.zeros(...)`, so the function
always returns float32 no matter what the caller asked for.

```
requested torch.bfloat16 -> got torch.float32   (before)
requested torch.bfloat16 -> got torch.bfloat16  (after)
```

The corrected form already exists in the tree, in the Quasar port of Llama 3.2 1B added by
#51337:

https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/models/experimental/llama32_1b_quasar/utility_functions.py#L93

That copy returns `result_tensor.to(dtype)` and carries a comment noting that `Tensor.to`
is not in-place. The fix was never brought back to the shared `models/common` version, so
every caller of the common helper still gets the wrong dtype. This PR applies the same
one-line fix to the canonical copy.

### Why it has not been noticed

Both current callers pass `dtype=torch.float32`:

- `tests/sweep_framework/sweeps/eltwise/unary/eqz/eqz.py:49`
- `tests/sweep_framework/sweeps/eltwise/unary/eqz/eqz_sharded.py:95`

float32 is exactly what the un-converted tensor already is, so the defect is invisible
today. It becomes visible the moment a caller asks for bfloat16 or float16, which is the
whole reason the parameter exists.

### Testing

The change is behaviour-preserving for both existing callers, since float32 in and float32
out is unchanged.

Verified the function directly for the three dtypes a caller would plausibly request, and
confirmed shape and zero-fraction behaviour are untouched:

```
requested torch.bfloat16  -> got torch.bfloat16   shape (4, 4)  zero_frac 0.06
requested torch.float16   -> got torch.float16    shape (4, 4)  zero_frac 0.06
requested torch.float32   -> got torch.float32    shape (4, 4)  zero_frac 0.06
```

items.body:
### PR Category
Bug fix

### Summary
Closes #55332.

On Blackhole a shift amount outside `[0, 31]` returned a wrong value from `bitwise_right_shift` instead of 0: a negative shift shifted left, so `8 >> -1` gave 16 and `1024 >> -8` gave 262144.

In `ckernel_sfpu_shift.h` the range guard passed a register selector (`p_sfpu::LCONST_0`) where the instruction modifier belongs and was missing the `TTI_SFPCOMPC` its left-shift sibling has, and the sign-extension block then ran on lanes the guard should have zeroed. This replaces that sequence with the SFPI implementation Wormhole already uses, which applies the guard last. `bitwise_left_shift` and `logical_right_shift` are untouched.

Verified on ttsim (Blackhole, `v0.79.0-dev20260903`): the 80 value/shift combinations from the issue go from 25 wrong to 0, the new test goes from 21 of 42 lanes non-zero to 0 on both `int32` and `uint32`, and the existing `test_bitwise_right_shift` passes before and after.

### Notes for reviewers
For negative values with an out-of-range shift the kernel contract, Wormhole and the left-shift sibling all give 0, while the registered golden (`torch.bitwise_right_shift`) saturates to -1. This change matches Wormhole rather than the golden, and the new test only asserts the positive-value cases where the two agree. Say the word if you would rather both architectures follow the golden.
